summary: Vendor prior art for a capacitor-bank-fed pulsed white LED strobe on a hard-limited supply. Closest analogue is TI TIDA-01081 (machine-vision LED flash): energy-storing capacitor bank on an intermediate rail plus a firmware-adjustable average input current limit, giving 40 W+ LED pulses from an 8-10 W input budget. Decay-tail and fade-in mechanisms are the switching driver's inductor, its output capacitance and its soft-start - a linear low-side pass element has none of the three, which is the case for the assigned topology. Cost of the linear stage is a linear-mode SOA problem (Infineon/Nexperia/TI hot-swap rules apply). Pulsed LED over-drive is NOT available at 5-200 ms pulse widths: vendor surge ratings are microsecond ratings, so the emitter must be DC-rated for 2.6 A.

decisions.what: Put the energy bank on the supply side of the drive stage and fit essentially zero capacitance across the LED string.
decisions.why: The bank buys peak power from a power-limited rail; capacitance across the string is what produces a post-turn-off decay tail. TI's design stores energy in the pre-boost output capacitors feeding the LED driver's input and runs the LED output with no output capacitor at all, choosing the buck topology precisely because it needs none.
decisions.source: TI TIDUDB6 (TIDA-01081) s2.4.1.1 and s2.4.1.3 bullet 5, https://www.ti.com/lit/ug/tidudb6/tidudb6.pdf ; TI TPS92515 datasheet SLUSBZ6A s9.2.1.7 'no output capacitance is required', Figure 15 'No Output Capacitor', https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/tps92515.pdf

decisions.what: Attribute the decay tail to the driver's inductor, its output capacitance and its soft-start - not to the LED. A linear low-side pass element eliminates all three, which is the strongest technical argument for the assigned topology.
decisions.why: TI states its hysteretic buck cannot meet 40-100 ns rise/fall 'based on the hysteretic operation alone. The buck inductor and its physical property of slowing down any change in current flow through the inductor is the reason for it', and separately credits the driver's PWM pin for switching 'without the delay or soft-start phases found in other DC/DC converters and LED drivers'. Phosphor persistence (YAG:Ce, tens of ns) is four orders below the 1 ms optical fall requirement and is not a limit.
decisions.source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.1, https://www.ti.com/lit/ug/tidudb6/tidudb6.pdf ; TI TPS92515 SLUSBZ6A s9.2.1.7. Phosphor decay figure is DERIVED/OPINION - order of magnitude only, no vendor datasheet cited.

decisions.what: Understand (but do not copy) the two-FET trick used to get 40-100 ns edges from a switching driver: a shunt FET across the string for instant ON after pre-charging the inductor, plus an active discharge FET into a lower-Vf parallel path for instant OFF, both close to the LEDs with dedicated gate drivers and independently tuned rise/fall.
decisions.why: TI: 'When this FET is switched off, the inductor current IL is steered immediately through the five LEDs, switching them on instantaneously', and the discharge path's 'voltage drop ... is much lower than the forward voltage of the LED string. This is why the LED current is instantaneously steered away from the LEDs towards this parallel path.' Drivers are UCC27511 with separate OUTH/OUTL for independent edge tuning.
decisions.source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.2 and s2.4.1.1 Table 8 states 1-5, https://www.ti.com/lit/ug/tidudb6/tidudb6.pdf

decisions.what: REJECT shunt-FET dimming for this board. Interrupt the string in series with the pass element instead.
decisions.why: Shunt-FET dimming is the standard automotive matrix-LED answer and TI supports it (10,000:1 range), but it works by keeping the converter current continuous - TI notes that active inductor discharge 'reduces the average power dissipation in the freewheeling diode and inductor compared to a pure shunt-FET dimming implementation', i.e. under pure shunt dimming full current keeps circulating and burning while the LED is dark. DERIVED: on a 0.99 J bank refilled from 8.5 W that would draw the same average energy lit or dark, collapsing the flash rate.
decisions.source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.2, https://www.ti.com/lit/ug/tidudb6/tidudb6.pdf ; TI TPS92515 SLUSBZ6A features / s8.3.4, https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/tps92515.pdf . Budget consequence is DERIVED.

decisions.what: Implement STR-REQ-04 sub-flash intensity as analogue amplitude control on the current-source reference. Accept the chromaticity consequence and verify it against the chosen emitter's published chromaticity-vs-current curve.
decisions.why: TI sets pulse amplitude with a DAC on the driver's IADJ analogue current-set pin; analogue dimming range is 200:1. Both major LED vendors publish the colour-vs-current curve (Cree 'Relative Chromaticity vs Current'; ams-OSRAM dCx,dCy = f(IF) on a +/-0.03 axis), so the STR-REQ-14 check is deterministic. Published measurement of phosphor-converted white shows <4-step MacAdam shift from 100% to 3% under both analogue and PWM dimming.
decisions.source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.1 (IADJ/VIADJ), https://www.ti.com/lit/ug/tidudb6/tidudb6.pdf ; Cree XHP70.3 CLD-DS266 Rev 11A 'Relative Chromaticity vs Current', https://downloads.cree-led.com/files/ds/x/XLamp-XHP70.3.pdf ; ams-OSRAM GW CSSRM3.HW v1.2 'Chromaticity Coordinate Shift dCx,dCy = f(IF)', https://look.ams-osram.com/m/55c5480864548464/original/GW-CSSRM3-HW.pdf ; Dyble/Narendran, SPIE 5941 (2005) - ACADEMIC, not vendor, https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2005SPIE.5941..291D/abstract

decisions.what: Treat the pass element as a linear-mode / SOA selection problem. Power dissipation is Vds*Ids and Rds(on) is irrelevant; the binding limit is the thermal-instability line, which applies only below the ZTC point.
decisions.why: Infineon: 'As the MOSFET is operated exclusively in linear mode, the RDS(on) of the MOSFET is completely irrelevant when calculating the power dissipation.' Instability criterion VDS * ZthJC(tpulse) * dIDS/dT > 1 requires a positive temperature coefficient of drain current, which occurs only for VGS below ZTC; below ZTC 'local hot spots will draw more current as they heat up ... Ultimately this results in thermal runaway and local destruction of the chip'. Nexperia names this the Spirito effect and adds that wider pulses trigger it at LOWER voltages - our pulses are 5-200 ms, i.e. wide.
decisions.source: Infineon AN 'Linear Mode Operation and Safe Operating Diagram of Power-MOSFETs' V1.1 May 2017, s1.1 and s2.1, https://www.infineon.com/dgdl/Infineon-ApplicationNote_Linear_Mode_Operation_Safe_Operation_Diagram_MOSFETs-AN-v01_00-EN.pdf?fileId=db3a30433e30e4bf013e3646e9381200 ; Nexperia IAN50006, https://www.nexperia.com/applications/interactive-app-notes/IAN50006_Power_MOSFETs_in_linear_mode

decisions.what: Pass-element selection rules: 100 V-class or higher, large package, low ZthJC, datasheet SOA curves that actually cover 10 ms and 100 ms, preferably an explicitly linear-mode-qualified family (Infineon Linear FET / Nexperia ASFET / IXYS Linear L2). Do NOT select on Rds(on).
decisions.why: Infineon: 'Thermal instability can be avoided by utilizing MOSFETs with low ZTC point. This means that MOSFETs of previous technology generations and/or higher voltage classes will be more suitable for this kind of application', because 'Modern power MOSFETs exhibit ever increasing transconductances and therefore also ZTC-points at higher VGS'. Nexperia independently: 'Newer technologies show generally worse linear mode capability', mitigated by lower junction-to-base thermal resistance, larger packages, older-generation technologies or its enhanced-SOA ASFET portfolio. The 100 V class is forced anyway by the 57 V worst-case rail (requirements s8.1).
decisions.source: Infineon AN s2.1 and s3, https://www.infineon.com/dgdl/Infineon-ApplicationNote_Linear_Mode_Operation_Safe_Operation_Diagram_MOSFETs-AN-v01_00-EN.pdf?fileId=db3a30433e30e4bf013e3646e9381200 ; Nexperia IAN50006, https://www.nexperia.com/applications/interactive-app-notes/IAN50006_Power_MOSFETs_in_linear_mode

decisions.what: Derate the SOA three ways before believing it: case temperature, repetition (duty cycle), and pulse width. Check TWO operating points - the flash (26 W at 10 V / 2.6 A, decaying, repetitive) and the cold-start bank charge (~12 W peak / ~6 W average for ~540 ms, single event).
decisions.why: TI hot-swap gives SOA(Tc) = SOA(25C) * (Tj,max - Tc)/(Tj,max - 25C), a log-log power-law interpolation SOA(t) = a*t^m between datasheet points, and a non-square-to-square pulse conversion. Infineon: datasheet SOA is at duty cycle D=0, so repetitive pulses require ZthJC = f(tp, D) instead of the single-pulse curve. Nexperia: of the three derating conventions, current scaling is the best Spirito approximation and the most conservative against measured data. Board ambient is 56-69 C (requirements s4), not 25 C.
decisions.source: TI SLVA673A 'Robust Hot Swap Design' s2.3.1-2.3.3, eq. 5 and eq. 6, Table 1, https://www.ti.com/lit/an/slva673a/slva673a.pdf ; Infineon AN s2.1 ; Nexperia IAN50006. The two operating-point numbers are DERIVED from requirements s3.2 and the 48->40 V window.

decisions.what: Do not rely on pulsed over-current. Select an emitter whose DC forward-current rating covers 2.6 A at the derated solder-point temperature. This closes STR-REQ-13: the pulsed derating curve is checked and it does not help at 5-200 ms.
decisions.why: Cree publishes no numeric pulse allowance and warns that repetitive over-current causes electromigration and eventual failure, that trade-offs 'may adversely affect efficiency, chromaticity and long-term reliability', and that operating outside published specs negates the warranty. ams-OSRAM's numeric surge rating is 2000 mA at t <= 10 us, D = 0.005 against an 1800 mA DC rating - i.e. +11% for ten microseconds. DERIVED: LED junction thermal time constants are milliseconds, so a 5-200 ms pulse is thermally a DC event. Existence proof (NOT a part recommendation): Cree XHP70.3 is DC-rated 3600 mA in the 12 V configuration with Rth j-to-solder-point 0.2 C/W and Vf 11.2-12.2 V at 1050 mA/85 C, so ~3 in series lands near the <=38 V budget at 2.6 A with no over-drive.
decisions.source: Cree CLD-AP60 Rev 4A 'Repetitive Pulsing', 'Summary', footnote 2, https://downloads.cree-led.com/files/da/x/XLamp-Pulsed-Current.pdf ; ams-OSRAM GW CSSRM3.HW v1.2 Maximum Ratings, https://look.ams-osram.com/m/55c5480864548464/original/GW-CSSRM3-HW.pdf ; Cree XHP70.3 CLD-DS266 Rev 11A Characteristics, https://downloads.cree-led.com/files/ds/x/XLamp-XHP70.3.pdf

decisions.what: Size the optical claim off the vendor's Relative Flux vs Current curve (droop), and derate the permissible forward current against solder-point temperature, not ambient. Both the sustained and the peak thermal case must pass (STR-REQ-15).
decisions.why: Cree publishes 'Relative Flux vs Current (TJ = 85 C)'; flux is sub-linear in current so 2.6 A does not buy 2.6x the lumens of 1.0 A. ams-OSRAM publishes 'Max. Permissible Forward Current IF = f(Ts)' against solder-point temperature; at the 56-69 C internal air of requirements s4 the permissible current is materially below the 25 C headline.
decisions.source: Cree XHP70.3 CLD-DS266 Rev 11A 'Relative Flux vs Current (TJ = 85 C)', https://downloads.cree-led.com/files/ds/x/XLamp-XHP70.3.pdf ; ams-OSRAM GW CSSRM3.HW v1.2 'Max. Permissible Forward Current IF = f(T)', https://look.ams-osram.com/m/55c5480864548464/original/GW-CSSRM3-HW.pdf

decisions.what: Build the charge path as a hot-swap with dv/dt (constant-inrush) gate-slew control, with a firmware-settable current limit - not a power-limit-only start-up.
decisions.why: TI: for large output capacitance a power-limit start-up 'can be impractical ... Eventually, there will be no FETs that can support such a requirement. An alternative is to limit the inrush current with a dv/dt control circuit ... Cdv/dt limits the slew rate of the gate and the output voltage, which in turn limits the inrush current', giving constant inrush with MOSFET power falling as Vout rises. TIDA-01081 is direct precedent for making the limit firmware-settable: 'The dual DAC of the common power block controls the adaptive current limit of the eFuse and of the pre-boost.'
decisions.source: TI SLVA673A s2.2.2, Figure 6, Figure 7, https://www.ti.com/lit/an/slva673a/slva673a.pdf ; TI TIDUDB6 s1 and s2.4.1.3, https://www.ti.com/lit/ug/tidudb6/tidudb6.pdf

decisions.what: Design the charge path against the PD's MINIMUM limits - 0.85 A current limit and 500 us foldback deglitch - not the 1.0 A / 800 us typicals quoted in the ICD. Recommend a charge-path limit at or below 0.6 A.
decisions.why: TPS2378 datasheet: current limit 0.85 / 1.0 / 1.2 A; inrush limit 100 / 140 / 180 mA; foldback threshold VRTN rising 11 / 12.3 / 13.6 V; foldback deglitch 500 / 800 / 1500 us. Text: 'If RTN ever exceeds about 12 V for longer than 800 us, then the TPS2378 returns to inrush limiting.' DERIVED: the trip is the voltage across the PD's pass FET held above threshold for longer than the deglitch, and holding the PD in current limit is what raises that voltage - so a 0.9 A charge path is inside the ICD's stated 1.0 A ceiling and can still fold a worst-case PD back to 140 mA and brown out the fixture.
decisions.source: TI TPS2378 datasheet, Electrical Characteristics table and s7.4.6 Inrush and Start-up, https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/tps2378.pdf

decisions.what: Linear (dissipative) charging is acceptable here and a switching pre-regulator is not worth its cost - but only because the steady-state top-up window is narrow. The cold start still pays the full 50 % penalty and is an SOA case.
decisions.why: TI implements its average input current limit 'in a quasi-lossless manner' via the switching pre-boost and contrasts it with the eFuse, which 'limits the current by controlling the ON-resistance of the internal pass FET. There is therefore an increase of losses and power dissipation in the eFuse as soon as the eFuse enters the current limit region.' DERIVED arithmetic: the pass element burns (Vsrc - Vc_mean)/Vsrc of delivered energy, = ~8.3 % over the 40->48 V top-up window but 50 % over a 0->48 V cold start (3.23 J stored, 3.23 J burnt), which over the 0.54 s cold-start time of requirements s3.2 is ~6 W average / 12 W peak in linear mode.
decisions.source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.3 (qualitative), https://www.ti.com/lit/ug/tidudb6/tidudb6.pdf ; arithmetic DERIVED from requirements s3.2 and ICD s6.4 figures

decisions.what: Specify the bank as a photo-flash / rapid-charge-discharge duty part, not a general-purpose electrolytic chosen on uF and volts. Conductive-polymer aluminium is not excluded by pulse current at 2.6 A.
decisions.why: Nichicon: 'For a circuit that repeats rapid charging / discharging of electricity, an appropriate capacitor that is capable of enduring such a condition must be used. Welding machines and photo flash are a few examples of products that contain such a circuit ... please consult Nichicon.' A 1-25 Hz strobe bank is squarely that duty. Same document caps polymer aluminium rush current at 10 A, and our 2.6 A discharge peak is inside that - useful because polymer is an SMD technology, which bears on the assembly-side question. Series-stacked electrolytics need balancing resistors.
decisions.source: Nichicon CAT.8100Z-2 'Application Guidelines for Aluminum Electrolytic Capacitors' s1(5) and s1(6), https://www.nichicon.co.jp/english/products/pdf/e-al_gui.pdf

layout_notes: L1 - The discontinuous high-di/dt loop on this board is bank(+) -> LED string -> sense resistor -> pass FET -> bank(-). Give it the discipline a buck's switch-node loop gets: minimum enclosed area, return directly under the outbound path, 'only large enough to connect the components without excessive heating'. Source: TI TPS92515 SLUSBZ6A s11.1 'Minimize discontinuous current loops'. Loop identification is DERIVED.

L2 - Kelvin the shunt. Four connections: two carrying current, two sensing. TI names the classic error explicitly: 'One of the most common mistakes in laying out the current sense resistor is connecting the current sense amplifier inputs to the current carrying trace instead of directly to the current sense resistor.' Four-wire Kelvin matters most below 0.5 mOhm; sense-pad placement (inner vs side) is itself an accuracy variable because many resistor datasheets do not state the manufacturing measurement point. Source: TI SBOA197 Figure 2 discussion, https://www.ti.com/lit/pdf/sboa197

L3 - Keep the sense pair tight and differential, do not run it parallel to the pulse path, and place the sense resistor as close as possible to the sensing amplifier's inputs. TI: 'The most sensitive loop contains the sense resistor (RSENSE). Place the sense resistor as close as possible to the CSN and VIN pins to maximize noise rejection', and minimise loops on all high-impedance control nodes. Source: TI TPS92515 SLUSBZ6A s11.1.

L4 - Separate the pulse return from the analogue/ADC return; join them only at the shunt's low side. The bank-voltage divider feeding ADC0 must reference that same quiet point. DERIVED from L2/L3 plus requirements s2.3 (ADC source impedance <= 10 kohm).

L5 - Gate drive: keep the driver / error amplifier next to the pass FET and return its ground to the FET source (shunt low side), not to the general plane, and keep the gate loop out of the pulse loop's field. TI places its steering FETs 'in close proximity to the LEDs' with dedicated UCC27511 drivers using separate OUTH/OUTL outputs so rise and fall speed can be tuned independently. Source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.2; application to a linear stage is DERIVED.

L6 - Remote LED module (requirements open question 4 default): the wiring harness is inside the pulse loop. Run the two conductors as a tight pair to hold loop inductance down, and do NOT add a bulk capacitor at the module - per D1 that capacitor is a decay tail. TI's guidance is the mirror image: when an output capacitor IS used with a remote load, place it at the LEDs 'to reduce the effects of parasitic inductance on the AC impedance of the capacitor'. Source: TI TPS92515 SLUSBZ6A s11.1.

L7 - Nothing may be added to the LED path for EMI reasons without re-measuring the optical edge. TI: 'The ferrite beads L6 and L7 and the snubber R130/C95 are used to improve EMI; however, these parts slow down the speed of switching the LEDs on and off. This speed is critical when using the design for ultra-short LED pulses.' Source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.2. Interacts with STR-REQ-11.

L8 - CONFLICT to resolve at layout: L1 wants the pulse loop tight, and bank(+) is a 48 V net carrying this project's board-wide 0.60 mm outer-layer clearance rule (requirements s8.1, IPC-2221B B2). Do NOT narrow the gap. Shrink the loop vertically instead - put the return directly beneath the outbound conductor on an adjacent layer, where the governing minimum is JLC's 0.127 mm and the HV requirement is free. DERIVED.

L9 - Probing these edges needs a ground spring, not a probe lead and alligator clip ('The small ground spring reduces significantly the noise, which can couple otherwise into the long ground lead of a standard probe configuration'). Compounded by requirements s8.4: the fixture floats at PoE potential, an earthed probe breaks PD detection outright, and every test point carries the carrier's silkscreen warning. Source: TI TIDUDB6 s3 (probe recommendation).
errata: E1 - Leakage glow defeats 'instant blackout'. TI fits a 100 uA pulldown because 'The high-side FET driver has a small leakage path to the output. Although very small (<<100 uA), the LEDs could glow if the current was not eliminated.' A high-power white LED at tens of microamps is visible in a dark room. Budget pass-element Idss, bleed path and ADC divider so no sub-milliamp path crosses the string when off; add a deliberate blackout shunt if one exists. Source: TI TPS92515 SLUSBZ6A s8.3.11.

E2 - The first flash after a long gap is the one that fades in. Machine-vision flash drivers hit 'output capacitor charge loss due to leakage, preventing a quick response when the LED is turned back on' after long off-times, fixed by trickle-charging the loop during the gap. STR-REQ-01 goes down to 1 Hz, so any sample-held or AC-coupled current reference, or any soft-start on the regulating loop, becomes a visible fade-in on the first flash of a phrase. Keep the reference DC-coupled and alive under ENABLE. Source: LED professional, 'LED Driver for High Power Machine Vision Flash', https://www.led-professional.com/resources-1/articles/led-driver-for-high-power-machine-vision-flash

E3 - 'Surge current' on an LED datasheet is a microsecond rating. ams-OSRAM GW CSSRM3.HW: IFS 2000 mA at t <= 10 us, D = 0.005, against 1800 mA DC. Do not read it as headroom for a millisecond flash. Source: ams-OSRAM GW CSSRM3.HW v1.2 Maximum Ratings.

E4 - Over-driving the LED voids the warranty and puts lifetime testing on us. Cree: 'Operating XLamp LEDs outside the published specifications negates the warranty', and 'Cree LED recommends that customers perform their own lifetime testing'. A 4-6 unit build has no lifetime-test budget. Source: Cree CLD-AP60 Rev 4A Summary and footnote 2.

E5 - Do not pick the pass element on Rds(on). Modern low-Rds(on) trench parts are the worst choice for linear mode (higher transconductance -> ZTC at higher VGS -> more of the operating range thermally unstable), and in continuous linear mode Rds(on) is 'completely irrelevant' to dissipation. Source: Infineon AN s1.1 and s3; Nexperia IAN50006.

E6 - Datasheet SOA curves do not apply as printed: they are single-pulse at Tc = 25 C, and this board is repetitive at Tc well above 25 C. Both derations are mandatory, and Nexperia adds that longer pulses trigger Spirito at LOWER voltages, so the 200 ms case is not a scaled 5 ms case. Source: Infineon AN s2.1; TI SLVA673A eq. 5; Nexperia IAN50006.

E7 - Design the charge path to the PD's minimum limits (0.85 A, 500 us deglitch, 11 V foldback threshold), not the typicals quoted in the ICD. See D12. Source: TI TPS2378 datasheet Electrical Characteristics.

E8 - A pass element still in current regulation can never charge the bank to the rail: it must hold some VDS, so the bank asymptotes below 48 V and flash energy is lost. The charge path must terminate by driving the FET fully enhanced (ohmic) once current falls below the limit, exactly as a hot-swap does. DERIVED, consistent with TI SLVA673A s2.2.1 and Infineon AN s1.1's three-state e-fuse description.

E9 - Cold start is an SOA event and it is larger than the flash: ~12 W peak, ~6 W average, ~540 ms in linear mode (DERIVED from requirements s3.2's 0.54 s cold-start at the af sustained limit). Easy to overlook because it is not the flash the board was designed around.

E10 - Repetitive charge/discharge needs a photo-flash-class capacitor; a general-purpose electrolytic chosen on uF and volts will not survive the duty. STR-REQ-08 already requires the ripple-current rating in the BOM. Source: Nichicon CAT.8100Z-2 s1(5).

E11 - Shunt-FET dimming does not reduce current drawn from the source. It is the standard automotive matrix-LED answer and the wrong answer on an 8.5 W budget. See D4. Source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.2 (freewheel-loss statement); budget consequence DERIVED.
E12 - EMI parts on the LED path (ferrite beads, snubbers) slow the optical edge. See L7. Source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.2.

E13 - Do not read TIDA-01081 as an endorsement of a buck for THIS board. TI opens by choosing a switching regulator for 'less power dissipation compared to any linear regulator approach', then spends two extra FETs, two gate drivers and a discharge network undoing the inductor's effect on the edges. See OPEN-1. Source: TI TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.1 and s2.4.1.2.
open: OPEN-1 - Source-vs-assignment conflict. TI states a switching regulator has 'the clear advantage of less power dissipation compared to any linear regulator approach' (TIDUDB6 s2.4.1.1), yet the assigned topology is a linear pass element. The situations differ: TI regulates from a FIXED 48.5 V rail into a 24 V string (~24 V of headroom to burn) whereas this board's bank droops 48 -> 40 V into a 38 V string (2-10 V, DERIVED ~14 % average loss), and the linear stage removes the inductor that STR-REQ-01/STR-REQ-11 make expensive. The price is the SOA burden of D6-D8. Surface to the architect rather than resolve silently.

OPEN-2 - Vendors disagree on whether a millisecond-scale pulse rating exists. Cree publishes none and disclaims warranty outside spec; ams-OSRAM's surge rating is microseconds-only; but TI reports the OSLON Black Flat it used is specified 1.5 A DC with 'data for the permissible pulse handling capability up to peak pulses of 2.5 A' (1.67x), on a different part. Availability of a ms-scale pulse curve is PER-PART, not per-vendor. Resolution rule for the component-scout: either select a part whose datasheet publishes a pulse-handling curve covering 5-200 ms, or stay inside the DC rating - do not interpolate between the two.

OPEN-3 - Is the PD ceiling 1.0 A (requirements s3.2 / ICD s8.2) or 0.85 A (TPS2378 datasheet minimum)? Deglitch likewise 800 us quoted vs 500 us minimum. Designing to typicals leaves no margin on a worst-case PD. Needs confirming with the carrier owner; until then design to 0.85 A / 500 us.

OPEN-4 - The analogue-dimming chromaticity evidence behind D5 is academic (SPIE 2005, <4-step MacAdam 100%->3%), not vendor. Datasheets publish the chromaticity-vs-current curve but state no acceptance limit. Once a specific emitter is chosen, re-check STR-REQ-14 against that part's own curve.

OPEN-5 - No vendor reference design was found for the exact combination of a linear pass element fed by a large capacitor bank at these pulse widths. TIDA-01081 is the closest, and it is a switching design. The linear-mode arithmetic in D6-D8 and D13 is therefore assembled from generic MOSFET/hot-swap primary sources rather than lifted from a proven strobe design - it should be treated as a design that needs bench verification, not a copied topology.
